claim.quote: The next form of alternate credibility is your background or your story.

action.text: Tell your background or story in a way that resonates with the target audience.
action.quote: by telling them my story, I'd resonated with them.

args.text: You lack testimonials or need alternative credibility.
args.quote: So what if you don't have testimonials?

unknowns: What parts of a background story to use are not specified.

existing_units.title: Professional drummer story creates a bond with musicians

claim.text: The source describes how mentioning his past as a professional drummer caused musicians to approach him and feel a bond.
claim.quote: if I mentioned the fact that I was I used to be a professional drummer a certain group of people would come up and find me at the end of the talk and mention the fact that they had also been a professional musician

claim.text: The source asserts that you have to resonate with the target audience, and telling your story did that.
claim.quote: You have to resonate with the target audience.

reasons: The excerpt explicitly asserts that people use a website's first impression to make broader judgments about the business and that perceived performance across every metric is higher purely because of that impression.
The source expressly says the two websites were for the same company and were a before-and-after comparison, while the preceding discussion identifies website B as the stronger-perceived version.
The warning, trigger, and stated inability to assess positive versus negative first-impression impact are directly stated in the excerpt.

The source recommends contacting Exposure Ninja for a free website and marketing review or using a site such as useresting.com to obtain an impartial perspective, following the warning directed at self-built-site owners.
The source directly states that a website resembling website A is a problem because people judge it negatively.

The excerpt says organizations the company had worked with should not be buried where visitors must dig for them, but should be front and center; it then describes using logos and naming those organizations in the above-the-fold section.
The source specifically describes testimonials that include both the company name and the testimonial giver's job role, and explains the value of that role-specific detail for relevant prospects.
The excerpt explicitly characterizes the relevant testimonials as before-and-after testimonials, with a prospect recognizing the before situation and seeking the stated after result.

The source presents awards the company had won and reviews it had received from Google as credibility elements, but the action omits the material availability/authenticity condition. It should specify displaying genuine awards and existing Google reviews rather than implying these elements can be used without having earned or received them.
The source supports placing case studies on service pages as well as a case-study page and says they can be used throughout the site.
However, it materially specifies that the service-page case studies concern the particular service offered on that page. The candidate omits this service-to-case-study matching requirement.
The source expressly asserts that case studies cannot be overused and calls them a powerful credibility-building tool.

The excerpt introduces nailing a customer's problem through hyperniching as the first alternative-credibility approach for businesses lacking testimonials, and states that sufficiently detailed problem description immediately builds credibility.
The palm-reader anecdote is stated in the source as an illustration that accurately describing someone's situation creates immediate credibility without needing testimonials or case studies.
The source explicitly presents a person's background or story as another form of alternative credibility and links telling a resonant story with building a sense of closeness with the audience.

The source states that mentioning the speaker's former professional drumming led musicians and other music-interested attendees to approach him, and explains that the shared element of his story created a bond.
The source directly says, "You have to resonate with the target audience," and uses the speaker's story as an example of doing so.

omissions.description: When placing case studies on service pages, match each case study to the particular service offered on that page.
omissions.quote: And these are case studies about this specific service that they offer.

omissions.description: Show case-study logos or client association even when visitors may not open the full case study, because the visible association itself is presented as credibility.
omissions.quote: We know that people aren't necessarily going to click through and read the full case study, but they don't need to for us to get the benefit of that credibility because just by seeing the logo and knowing that that business has worked with us on this particular thing gives us that credibility, doesn't it?

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-discussion and ends mid-sentence, so the full framing and the unfinished guidance on how to tell a personal story are unavailable.
The website A/B comparison and page-layout examples depend partly on visuals not included in the text; the excerpt does not define the visual attributes that distinguish the examples.
The excerpt provides no respondent counts, testing protocol, measurement method, or underlying data for claims about first-impression perceptions or case-study-page traffic.
The credibility and platform-related statements are presenter assertions and examples in this excerpt; they are not accompanied by independent verification or operational details.
